title: Head arrangements and playing the blues in Bogalusa
summary: Desvigne says the band knew its arrangements by memory and tells of a Bogalusa crowd that only danced when they played the blues.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Can you ask once more about some of your arrangements with your big band? Did you all ever just do without the music altogether on any number and just play a whole head arrangement with a big ten or twelve piece band, or did you always have music?

Well, no, we didn't do that so much. We knew the arrangements as far as that's concerned. We knew them. Yeah, we knew them, you see? But we could sit there and play most of our, the whole program that night, you see? Because we remembered all the things by playing them, you see? Remember that.
Yeah, I was just wondering if they'd ever say, for instance, call it blues, like in B flat or something, and then they just play.
Oh, well that was just the blues, yeah, at times. Yeah, yeah, just the blues, yeah.
Yeah, and the whole band could improvise or maybe-
Well, we played an engagement in a place they call Bugaloosa in Louisiana.

The honky-tonk. Okay. We got up there and start playing our big arrangements. Nobody want to dance. Nobody. They say, this band come from New York. This is the music they're playing. They come from New York. We don't want that kind of music. One fellow in the band said, let's play the blues. So when we played the blues, then they all got out and started hollering, and that's what they wanted, the blues. That's right. Yeah.
The other than the band did things like that too.
